messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malia Thongchanh is a fifty-one-year-old Laotian American dentist who presented for an initial psychological evaluation reporting significant and persistent distress following a prolonged stalking experience that began approximately three years ago. Married and working full-time in a private dental practice in a mid-sized Midwestern city, she described herself before the stalking as confident and professionally accomplished — someone who had built her career and family life with deliberate care. That sense of safety collapsed over the eighteen months during which a former patient tracked her movements, appeared outside her clinic, left packages at her home, and sent messages that escalated from unsettling to explicitly threatening. What made the experience particularly destabilizing was not any single incident but the cumulative erosion of her ability to trust her own environment: she never knew when he would appear, and the spaces she had considered most hers — her waiting room, her car, her front porch — became sites of potential danger. When police were eventually involved, their response felt procedurally distant and practically insufficient, and she was left with the enduring impression that no external authority could actually guarantee her safety. A restraining order was obtained, the stalking eventually ceased, and by most external measures the threat is over. Malia does not experience it that way.

In the period following the stalking, she noticed that certain things in her ordinary life had become impossible to move through without a surge of alarm. A particular kind of slow, ambient pop song — the type that had played in her clinic's waiting room during the months the stalker was a patient — could stop her mid-task and flood her with a sense of immediate danger that felt entirely real, regardless of where she was. Encountering media coverage of stalking cases, true-crime content, or even news segments about harassment produced the same effect: a sudden, involuntary shift in which the present moment seemed to collapse into the worst period of her life. Most acutely, the sight of uniformed police officers — once a neutral or even reassuring presence — now triggered the same visceral alarm, her body registering their presence as evidence that something threatening was already happening. Each of these encounters reliably pulls Malia back into a state of perceived threat, and once that state is activated, it does not resolve quickly. She finds it essentially impossible to accept reassurance when she is in that condition; even her husband's calm, measured insistence that she is safe cannot reach her, because she has come to believe, at a level that feels more like knowledge than fear, that safety is not something others can verify on her behalf.

That conviction now organizes much of her daily behavior. At her dental practice — where she spends the majority of her waking hours — she has quietly restructured her environment around the management of perceived threat. She no longer uses the break room when other staff are present, preferring instead to eat at her desk with her back against the wall of her private office, from which she can see the hallway and both entry points to her suite. In the reception area, she has developed a habit of scanning every new patient's face before approaching, and she has repositioned her chair at the front consultation desk so that she sits with solid cabinetry behind her. These arrangements feel not like preferences but like necessities — the minimum conditions under which she can function. When a song comes through the office speaker system that resembles the ones from that period, or when a patient mentions something that touches on the media coverage she tries to avoid, the threat response returns immediately, and no amount of rational self-talk or collegial reassurance interrupts it.

What finally brought Malia to seek help was a moment several weeks ago when a police officer came to her building to respond to an unrelated incident in an adjacent office. She saw him in the corridor, felt the alarm cascade through her, and spent the remainder of the afternoon unable to complete patient procedures without her hands trembling. She told her office manager she had a migraine. She is most afraid that this will never change — that she has permanently lost the capacity to feel safe anywhere — and most hoping, tentatively, that someone can help her understand why her mind continues to insist the danger is still present.
